source_text: Sed quomodo funditus euertetur antichristus, nisi ceteris quoque iniectionibus eius elidendis locus detur. relaxata praescriptionum defensione? accedamus igitur iam hinc ad ipsam dei personam, uel potius umbram et phantasma secundum Christum ipsius. per idque examinetur, per quod creatori praefertur. et utique erunt regulae certae ad examinandam dei bonitatem. sed prius est, ut inueniam illam et adprehendam. et ita ad regulas perducam. cum enim circumspicio tempora, nusquam est a primordio materiarum et introitu causarum. cum quibus debuerat inueniri, exinde agens, quo agere habuit. erat enim iam et mors et aculeus mortis, delictum, et ipsa malitia creatoris. aduersus quam subuenire deberet alterius dei bonitas, t primae huic regulae diuinae bonitatis occurrens, si se naturalem probaret, statim succurrens, ut causa coepit. omnia enim in deo naturalia et ingenita esse debebunt, ut sint aeterna, secundum statum ipsius, ne obuenticia et extranea reputentur ac per hoc temporalia et aeternitatis aliena. ita et bonitas perennis et iugis exigetur in deo, quae in thesauris naturalium proprietatum reposita et parata antecederet causas et materias suas, et primam quamque susciperet, non despiceret et destitueret, si antecedebat. denique non minus et hic quaeram, cur non a primordio operata sit bonitas eius, quam de ipso quaesiuimus, cur non a primordio sit reuelatus? quidni? qui per bonitatem reuelari haberet, si qui fuisset. non posse quid deo non licet, nedum naturalibus suis fungi. quae si continentur, quo minus currant, naturalia non erunt. et otium enim sui natura non nouit; hinc censetur, si agat. sic nec noluisse uidebitur exercere bonitatem, interim naturae nomine. natura enim se non potest nolle, quae se ita dirigit, ut, si cessauerit, non sit. sed cessauit aliquando in deo Marcionis de opere bonitas: ergo non fuit naturalis bonitas, quae potuit aliquando cessasse, quod naturalibus non licet. et si non erit naturalis, iam nec aeterna credenda nec deo par. quia non aeterna, dum non naturalis, quae denique nullam sui perpetuitatem aut de praeterito constituat aut de futuro repromittat. nam ut a primordio non fuit, et in finem sine dubio non erit. potest enim et non esse quandoque, sicut non fuit aliquando. igitur cum constet in primordio cessasse bonitatem dei illius — (non) enim a primordio liberauit hominem — et uoluntate potius eam quam infirmitate cessasse, iam uoluntas subpressae bonitatis finis inuenietur malignitatis. quid enim tam malignum quam nolle prodesse cum possis,, quam utilitatem cruciare, quam iniuriam sinere? totum denique creatoris elogium in illum rescribetur, qui saeuitias eius i bonitatis suae mora iuuit. nam in cuius manu est quid ne fiat, eius iam deputatur, cum fit. homo damnatur in mortem ob unius arbusculae delibationem, et exinde proficiunt delicta cum poenis et pereunt iam omnes, qui paradisi nullum caespitem norunt. et hoc melior aliqui deus aut nescit aut sustinet? si ut ex hoc melior inueniretur, quanto creator deterior haberetur. satis et in isto consilio malitiosus, qui et illum uoluit oneratum, operationibus eius admissis, et saeculum in uexatione detinuit. quid de tali medico iudicabis, qui nutriat morbum mora praesidii et periculum extendat dilatione remedii, quo pretiosius aut famosius curet? talis et in deum Marcionis dicenda sententia est, mali permissorem, iniuriae fautorem, gratiae lenocinatorem, benignitatis praeuaricatorem, quam non statim causae suae exhibuit; plane exhibiturus, si natura bonus et non accessione, si ingenio optimus et non disciplina, si ab aeuo deus et non a Tiberio, immo, quod uerius, a Cerdone et Marcione. Tiberio nunc deus ille praestiterit, ut imperio eius diuina bonitas in terris dedicaretur,
pass_a_gloss: But how will antichrist be completely overthrown, unless also other injections of his are to be destroyed, with the defense of prescriptions relaxed? Let us approach, therefore, from here the very person of God, or rather the shadow and phantom according to Christ himself. And let it be examined through that by which it is preferred to the creator. And certainly there will be certain rules for examining the goodness of God. But first, it is necessary that I find and apprehend it, and thus lead to the rules. For when I look around at times, it is nowhere from the beginning of matters and the introduction of causes. With which it ought to have been found, from then on acting, since it had to act. For already there was death and the sting of death, transgression, and the malice itself of the creator. Against which the goodness of another God ought to have come to aid, as the first rule of divine goodness occurring, if it proved itself natural, immediately assisting, as the cause began. For all things in God ought to be natural and innate, so that they may be eternal, according to his state, lest they be considered adventitious and foreign, and for this reason temporal and alien to eternity. Thus also the goodness is required to be perpetual and constant in God, which, deposited and prepared in the treasures of natural properties, would precede its causes and matters, and would undertake the first of each, not despising and abandoning, if it preceded. Finally, I will also ask here, why his goodness did not operate from the beginning, just as we asked about him, why he was not revealed from the beginning? Why not? For he who was to be revealed through goodness, if he existed. It is not possible for God not to be able, much less to be unable to use his natural properties. If these are contained, why do they not run, will they not be natural? For even inactivity is not known by his nature; hence it is judged, if he acts. Thus it will not seem that he was unwilling to exercise goodness, meanwhile by the name of nature. For nature cannot be unwilling, which directs itself in such a way that, if it ceases, it is not. But the goodness in the God of Marcion ceased from work at some time; therefore, it was not natural goodness, which was able to have ceased at some time, which is not permitted to natural things. And if it is not natural, it is not to be believed eternal, nor equal to God. Because it is not eternal, since it is not natural, which finally constitutes no perpetuity of itself, either from the past or promised from the future. For just as it was not from the beginning, and in the end it will certainly not be. For it is able not to be at some time, just as it was not at some time. Therefore, since it is established that the goodness of that God ceased from the beginning — for it did not free man from the beginning — and it ceased by will rather than weakness, already the will of suppressed goodness will be found to be the end of malice. For what is as malicious as not to wish to benefit when you can, as to torture utility, as to allow injury? Finally, the whole eulogy of the creator will be rewritten to him, who helped his savagery with the delay of his goodness. For in whose hand it is what is not done, it is already attributed to him, when it is done. Man is condemned to death for the tasting of one little tree, and from then on transgressions proceed with punishments, and all who know no grass of paradise already perish. And does some better God either not know or tolerate this? If so that from this he might be found better, how much worse the creator would be considered. It is enough that in this counsel he is malicious, who also willed that he be burdened, with his operations admitted, and the world detained in vexation. What will you judge about such a doctor, who nourishes disease by the delay of aid and extends danger by the prolongation of remedy, so that he may treat more precious or famous cases? Such a sentence is to be said also about the God of Marcion, the permitter of evil, the favorer of injury, the pimp of grace, the transgressor of benignity, which he did not immediately exhibit to his cause; he would exhibit, if he were good by nature and not by acquisition, if he were optimal by genius and not by discipline, if he were God from eternity and not from Tiberius, indeed, what is truer, from Cerdo and Marcion. Now that God will have surpassed Tiberius, so that divine goodness might be dedicated on earth by his empire,
pass_b_english: How can Antichrist be utterly overthrown unless we are also given ground to demolish his other injections, now that the defense of prescriptions has been relaxed? Let us move on, then, to the very person of God — or rather, to the shadow and phantom that passes for Christ. He must be examined by the very standard by which he is preferred to the Creator. There will certainly be fixed rules for testing the goodness of God. But first I must find and seize that goodness, and only then bring it to the rules. For when I scan the timeline, it is nowhere to be found from the beginning of matter and the entrance of causes. It ought to have been present with them, acting from that point onward, since it had the obligation to act. Already there were death and the sting of death, transgression, and the Creator's own malice (Gen 2:17). Against these the goodness of another God ought to have rushed to help, presenting itself as the first rule of divine goodness — if it proved natural, it would have assisted immediately, right when the cause began. Everything in God ought to be natural and innate, so that it may be eternal, in keeping with his own state; otherwise it would be judged adventitious and alien, and therefore temporal and foreign to eternity. So too a perpetual, constant goodness is demanded in God — one stored and ready in the treasury of natural properties, preceding its own causes and materials, embracing each first occasion, not despising or abandoning it, if indeed it came first. Finally I must also ask here: why did his goodness not operate from the beginning, just as we asked why he himself was not revealed from the beginning? Why not? The one who was to be revealed through goodness, if he existed at all. It is impossible for God to be unable to do anything, much less to fail to exercise his own natural properties. If those properties are held in check, why do they not run? Then they would not be natural. For even inactivity is unknown to his nature; hence the verdict: if he acts. Thus it will not appear that he was unwilling to exercise goodness, meanwhile sheltering behind the name of nature. Nature cannot be unwilling — it directs itself so that if it ceases, it ceases to be. But the goodness in Marcion's God once ceased from work; therefore it was not natural goodness, which could have ceased at some point, something natural things are not permitted to do. And if it is not natural, it is no longer to be believed eternal or equal to God. Because it is not eternal, since it is not natural — a thing that finally guarantees no perpetuity for itself, neither from the past nor promised for the future. For just as it did not exist from the beginning, it certainly will not exist at the end. It is able not to be at some time, just as it once was not. Therefore, since it is established that the goodness of that God ceased from the beginning — for it did not free man from the beginning — and it ceased by will rather than weakness, the will that suppressed that goodness will be exposed as the end of malice. What is more malicious than refusing to benefit when you can, than torturing utility, than allowing injury? The whole eulogy of the Creator will be rewritten onto the one who abetted the Creator's savagery by delaying his own goodness. For whatever is not done lies in whose hand? It is already charged to him when it is done. Man is condemned to death for tasting one little tree; from then on transgressions advance with punishments, and all who never knew a blade of grass in paradise already perish (Gen 2:17). And does some better God either not know or tolerate this? If the purpose was that he might be found better by contrast, how much worse must the Creator be judged? It is enough that he is malicious in this scheme, who also willed that the Creator be burdened, admitted his operations, and held the world in vexation. What verdict will you pass on a doctor who feeds the disease by delaying aid and stretches out the danger by prolonging the remedy, so that he may cure more precious or famous cases? Such a sentence must also be pronounced on Marcion's God: the permitter of evil, the favorer of injury, the pimp of grace, the betrayer of benignity — which he did not immediately display for his cause. He would have displayed it if he were good by nature and not by acquisition, if he were optimal by genius and not by discipline, if he were God from eternity and not from Tiberius — indeed, what is truer, from Cerdo and Marcion. Now that God has outdone Tiberius, so that divine goodness might be dedicated on earth by his empire.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the nature of God's goodness and the critique of Marcion's deity. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin. Scripture citations (Gen 2:17) correctly identify the allusions to the tree and the sting of death. The title 'God's Goodness and Timing' accurately reflects the thought of the chapter.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key theological arguments. The inline citations match the content of the Latin passage.
